chunks: From him, from one of his companions, raising it (to the Imam), he said:

You should say after Fajr prayer: 'O Allah, to You belongs all praise, an eternal praise with Your eternity, and to You belongs all praise, a praise with no end until Your pleasure, and to You belongs all praise, a praise with no limit until Your will, and to You belongs all praise, a praise for its speaker no reward except Your pleasure. O Allah, to You belongs all praise, and to You is the complaint, and You are the One asked for help. O Allah, to You belongs all praise as You are worthy of it. All praise is for Allah with all His praises, upon all His bounties, until the praise reaches where my Lord loves and is pleased.'

And you should say after Fajr, before you speak: 'All praise is for Allah, filling the scale and the limit of pleasure and the weight of the Throne. And Glory be to Allah, filling the scale and the limit of pleasure and the weight of the Throne. And Allah is the Greatest, filling the scale and the limit of pleasure and the weight of the Throne. And there is no god but Allah, filling the scale and the limit of pleasure and the weight of the Throne.' Repeat that four times.

Then you should say: 'O Allah, I ask You the asking of the humble slave, that You send prayers upon Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, and that You forgive our sins and fulfill our needs in this world and the Hereafter, with ease from You and well-being.'

key_terms.مَسْأَلَةَ الْعَبْدِ الذَّلِيلِ: The asking of the humble servant
key_terms.مِلْءَ الْمِيزَانِ: Filling the scale (a measure of abundance)

ai.seo_question: What is the recommended supplication and dhikr to recite after the Fajr prayer according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: In Shia tradition, this supplication from Al-Kafi is highly regarded for its cosmic scale, linking human praise to the metaphysical realities of the Miizan (Scale), Ridwan (Divine Pleasure), and Arsh (Throne). The rhythmic repetition of the four key phrases serves as a comprehensive dhikr that encapsulates gratitude, glorification, magnification, and monotheism, reflecting the Shia emphasis on the interconnection between the believer's worship and the divine attributes. It concludes with a humble plea for both worldly ease and spiritual salvation, embodying the dual nature of Islamic supplication.
